paragraphs: The Chesed LaAlafim writes that one should say all the details of the confession (vidui) even though he did not do the things mentioned in it, because all of Israel are one body and all are guarantors for one another, and especially if it was in his power to protest and he did not protest, in which case it is called by his name — as our Sages, of blessed memory, wrote in the Gemara (Shabbat 54b) about the cow of Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah that used to go out with a strap between its horns: it was not his but his neighbor's, and since he did not protest it, it is called by his name. Furthermore, one must also confess for what he sinned in previous incarnations (gilgulim) as well, and who knows what he did — perhaps he transgressed all these things. Therefore the confession text says 'we have sinned, we and our fathers,' meaning the previous incarnations, which are called 'fathers' to this body that he is now in. And there is yet another reason for saying the entire confession: a person is judged according to what he is — for we find it written of Reuben (Genesis 35:22), 'and he lay with Bilhah,' because he disturbed his father's bed [arrangements]; and regarding the sons of Eli, that they 'lay with the women' (I Samuel 2:22), because they delayed their [sacrificial] nests; and the sons of Samuel turned aside after gain, because they asked for their portion with their own mouths (Shabbat 56a); and it is written of King David, peace be upon him, the sin of Bat-Sheva, even though she was divorced [from Uriah in intent], had immersed from her state of niddah, and had waited three months for verification (Sanhedrin 106–107). And furthermore, there are transgressions that a person treads underfoot [treats as insignificant] which are in fact considered severe — as our Sages of blessed memory taught: one who whitens [shames] his fellow's face is as though he shed blood (Bava Metzia 58–59); one who becomes angry is as though he worshipped idols (Zohar I, 27b); and one who is arrogant is as though he worshipped idols (Sotah 4–5) — and many more like these. Therefore, for all these reasons, a person must say all the details of the confession, as mentioned there.

clarification.explanation: One should say all the details of the confession, even for things he did not do, for several reasons: (a) All of Israel are one body and all are guarantors for one another, and especially if it was in his power to protest his fellow's [wrongdoing] and he did not protest, this is also counted in his name (as with Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah's atonement-cow in the Gemara, which was not his but his neighbor's, and since he did not protest, it was called by his name). (b) A person must also confess for what he sinned in previous incarnations — and who knows what he did; therefore we say 'we have sinned, we and our fathers,' meaning the previous incarnations are called 'fathers' to this body. (c) A person is judged according to his level, and for the righteous the standard of judgment is exacting to a hairsbreadth (as with Reuben, the sons of Eli, the sons of Samuel, and the sin of Bat-Sheva that was written of David even though she was divorced and had immersed). (d) There are transgressions that a person 'treads underfoot' and considers minor in his own eyes, but which are in truth severe — as our Sages said: one who shames his fellow's face is as though he shed blood; one who becomes angry is as though he worshipped idols; and one who is arrogant is as though he worshipped idols. For all these reasons, one should say all the details of the confession.
takeaways: One says all the details of the confession even for things he did not do — since all Israel are guarantors for one another, and one who did not protest [a wrong] is counted as though he had done it.
Also because of sins from previous incarnations ('our fathers'), because a person is judged according to his own level, and because of seemingly minor transgressions that are in fact severe.

paragraphs: Before the confession one should say, 'But we have sinned, we have transgressed, we have committed iniquity — we, our fathers, and the members of our household,' as is written in the siddur of our teacher the Rashash, of blessed memory. And one should likewise add, for the five letters that have final forms (mem, nun, tzadi, peh, khaf — 'MaNTzPaKh'), saying: 'We have lied, we have become angry, we have rebelled, we have defied Your words, we have blasphemed, we have committed adultery, we have transgressed, we have caused blemish, we have oppressed, we have grieved father and mother' — and so it is in the siddur of our teacher the Rashash, of blessed memory.

clarification.explanation: Before the confession itself one should say, 'But we have sinned, we have transgressed, we have committed iniquity — we, our fathers, and the members of our household,' as brought in the siddur of the Rashash. One should also add a further confession text corresponding to the five final-form letters (MaNTzPaKh), containing expressions such as 'we have lied, we have become angry, we have rebelled, we have defied Your words, we have blasphemed, we have committed adultery, we have transgressed, we have caused blemish, we have oppressed, we have grieved father and mother' — and so it is in the siddur of the Rashash.
takeaways: Before the confession one says an opening formula ('But we have sinned'), and adds a further confession built on the letters MaNTzPaKh, as brought in the siddur of the Rashash.

paragraphs: At the time of the confession, one should strike gently with the right hand, curled like a fist, upon the heart, which stands on the left side — one strike for each word of the confession — as mentioned in Sha'ar HaKavanot. It is already known that the location of the heart is beneath the breast, about four or five fingers' breadth toward the front. Every person should be careful to strike there, upon the heart, and not like those who strike above the breast or upon the breast itself, for that is not the location of the heart. The simple reason for striking upon the heart is to indicate that the heart caused him all these sins; but in truth the primary reason is not this — rather there is a hidden reason according to the esoteric teaching (Kabbalah), as explained in the words of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, in Sha'ar HaKavanot, that a person effects a great rectification (tikkun) through this striking upon the heart.

clarification.explanation: At the time of saying the confession one should strike with the right hand, curled like a fist, upon the heart which is on the left side — gentle strikes, one strike for every word of the confession. The location of the heart is beneath the chest, about four to five fingers' breadth inward, and one must be careful to strike exactly there and not above the chest or on the chest itself, for that is not the location of the heart. The simple reason is that the heart caused all these sins; but the true reason is esoteric, as explained in the words of the Ari, of blessed memory, that the striking upon the heart effects a great rectification.
takeaways: During the confession one strikes gently with the right hand upon the heart (beneath the chest, not above it or on it directly), one strike for each word — by virtue of a deep esoteric rectification beyond the simple reason.

paragraphs: Immediately after the confession one should say Vaya'avor and the Thirteen Attributes [of Mercy], and one must say them with intention of the heart, calmly and unhurriedly. I found it written that one should count his Thirteen Attributes and pass them over his fingers, in the manner of counting the eleven spice-ingredients of the incense — and this is a fine and proper custom. So I myself practice, for there is great benefit in this for concentration and intention, and the counting itself indicates the greatness and importance of the matter. Some are meticulous, when saying the Thirteen Attributes, to visualize their letters as though seeing them written before them in the siddur, one by one in their order, following the view of the Gaon Rabbi Chaim Mo'alezin, of blessed memory, regarding the Amidah prayer — and this too is a fine custom. But due to our many sins, the prayer leader and the congregation rush greatly through their recitation, and one who follows this practice [of careful intention] must linger much longer over their recitation; therefore let him do what he is able to do. And I wrote in my small book Makabtzi'el that if a person says the Thirteen Attributes with the congregation and they rush to finish while he is still in the middle, there is no harm in this — he is still considered as reciting them with the congregation, since he began them together with the congregation.

clarification.explanation: Immediately after the confession one says 'Vaya'avor' and the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy, and one should say them with intention of the heart, calmly and unhurriedly. Some are accustomed to count the Thirteen Attributes on their fingers, in the manner of counting the eleven spice-ingredients of the incense — a fine and proper custom, both for the benefit of concentration and intention, and because the counting itself expresses the importance of the matter. Some are even more meticulous and mentally visualize the letters of the Attributes as though they see them written before them in the siddur, one by one in order. It is regrettable that the prayer leader and the congregation rush greatly through their recitation, and one who is able should linger longer over them. If a person says the Thirteen Attributes together with the congregation, and the congregation rushes to finish while he is still in the middle, there is nothing wrong with this — he is still considered to have said them with the congregation, since he began together with them.
takeaways: One should say the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy calmly, with intention and without haste — not rushed as most of the congregation tends to do; a fine custom is to count them on one's fingers.
One who began reciting them together with the congregation is considered to have said them with the congregation, even if the congregation finishes before him.

paragraphs: Immediately after the confession and the recitation of the Thirteen Attributes, one should perform Nefilat Apayim (the falling upon the face) right away, for these three must be adjacent to one another. This is because through the saying of the confession, the Accuser takes his portion at the time of the confession and departs, separating from the place of holiness; and then two kinds of unions are effected above, in two aspects — one at the time of saying the Thirteen Attributes and the other at the time of Nefilat Apayim — and 'a stranger shall not come near' to the place of the Sanctuary to defile the Dwelling of the Lord, Heaven forbid, as mentioned in Sha'ar HaKavanot. Therefore, even on Mondays and Thursdays, one should not interrupt between the confession and Nefilat Apayim with the additional supplications recited on those days; rather, they should say Nefilat Apayim immediately, and afterward stand and say those supplications, from 'E-l Melekh' etc. to the end. Here in our city, Baghdad, the custom from ancient times was to say all the additional supplications on Mondays and Thursdays before Nefilat Apayim; but, praised be God, we abolished this custom and instituted saying Nefilat Apayim first, as our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, wrote.

clarification.explanation: After the confession and the Thirteen Attributes one must perform Nefilat Apayim immediately, because these three parts must be adjacent to one another. The reason: through the recitation of the confession, the Accuser (the Satan) takes his portion and withdraws from the place of holiness, and then two kinds of spiritual 'unions' are effected above — one at the time of saying the Thirteen Attributes, and the second at the time of Nefilat Apayim — and the 'stranger' (the husk/kelipah) cannot approach to defile the place of holiness. Therefore, even on Mondays and Thursdays, when additional supplications are added, one should not interrupt between the confession and Nefilat Apayim; rather one says Nefilat Apayim immediately, and only afterward stands and says the additional supplications ('E-l Melekh' etc.). In Baghdad the custom from ancient times was to say all the additional supplications on Mondays and Thursdays before Nefilat Apayim, but the Ben Ish Chai abolished this custom and instituted saying Nefilat Apayim first, as the Ari, of blessed memory, wrote.
takeaways: The confession, the Thirteen Attributes, and Nefilat Apayim must be said in one uninterrupted sequence, even on Mondays and Thursdays with their additional supplications.
The Ben Ish Chai changed the old local custom of Baghdad so that Nefilat Apayim is said immediately after the Attributes, before the additional supplications.

paragraphs: On the days when the confession, the Thirteen Attributes, and Nefilat Apayim are not said, the unions are certainly still effected above, but they occur by themselves, by virtue of the holiness of those days — so it is commonly said in the mouths of the Rabbis, the Kabbalists, of blessed memory. And I heard it said that the custom of the pious ones is to have this in mind only through thought, just as it is their way to have in mind, through thought alone, every commandment that is deferred on account of the Sabbath, such as the blowing of the shofar and the taking of the lulav. And if you should ask: on ordinary weekdays when confession and Nefilat Apayim were not said because there was a groom [celebrating his wedding week] or a circumcision in the synagogue — how are the unions above completed through the prayer of that congregation which prayed in that synagogue? The answer to this is that the prayer of that congregation is completed from the prayer of another congregation that did say confession and Nefilat Apayim, since ultimately the prayers of all the congregations are included with one another and rise together. And in the holy book Makabtzi'el I strengthened this reasoning from what Rabbi Chaim Vital, of blessed memory, wrote in Sha'ar HaKavanot in the discourse on the Torah scroll — and this is his language: 'For a long time my teacher [the Ari], of blessed memory, prayed in his house with a quorum of ten, and did not concern himself that there be a Torah scroll there to read from, whether on a weekday or on Shabbat' — end of his language. And how could the prayer of our teacher, the light of Israel, be lacking, Heaven forbid, the illuminations of the secret of the opening of the Ark, the Torah scroll, and the Torah reading? Rather, one must say that he relied in this on the other congregations that were bringing out a Torah scroll on those very days — for what is done in the other congregations benefits his congregation as well, since everything is included together. And in this manner I say that one who prays with the congregation and prolonged his own prayer and did not hear the repetition [of the Amidah by the prayer leader] — his prayer, too, is complete by virtue of the secret of the repetition, since it is included with the prayer of that congregation, and this is even better, since in truth he is praying together with them.

And know that in the holy book Makabtzi'el I brought the words of Rav Emet LeYa'akov, in Sefat Emet, page 102, column 4, regarding a question that was asked of the pious Rabbi, Zemirat HaAretz, concerning days on which Nefilat Apayim is not said due to custom — such as the days after Passover and after Sukkot, and likewise the days of a circumcision or a groom, and the like — since the omission of Nefilat Apayim on these days is not mentioned in the words of our Sages of blessed memory. And [Rav Emet LeYa'akov] who fears the word of the Lord and who has entered the secret of the Lord wrote that one should say Vaya'avor and Nefilat Apayim privately, between himself and [God] — see there. But I, the servant [of God, i.e., the author], had reservations about his words, and also had reservations about what he proved from Rosh Chodesh, and likewise had reservations about the opinion of Rav Emet LeYa'akov, who innovated on his own to have this in mind during the blessing 'Sim Shalom.' Only regarding what he wrote — to have it in mind through thought alone — did I agree, and blessing shall come upon him. And our beloved friend, the Gaon and pious Rabbi, Mahara Mani, may his Rock and Redeemer preserve him, wrote to me that he found from the mouth of the pious Rabbi, HaYeRA, of blessed memory, who wrote — and this is his language: 'It is an ancient custom in Beit El, may it be built and established, to have all the intentions in mind, in the heart, between the [prayer leader's] repetition and the Kaddish' — end [of his words].

clarification.explanation:
On days when confession, the Thirteen Attributes, and Nefilat Apayim are not said, the [spiritual] unions above still occur, but they occur by themselves, by virtue of the holiness of those days (as the Kabbalists say). And the Ben Ish Chai heard that the custom of the pious is to have this in mind through thought alone — just as it is their way to mentally intend every commandment that is deferred because of Shabbat, such as blowing the shofar or taking the lulav.
And if you should ask: on a plain weekday when confession and Nefilat Apayim were not said because there was a groom or a circumcision in the synagogue — how are the unions above completed from that congregation's prayer? The answer: that congregation's prayer is completed from the prayer of another congregation that did say confession and Nefilat Apayim, since ultimately all the congregations' prayers are joined together and rise as one. He also brought a proof from the words of Rabbi Chaim Vital, of blessed memory (Sha'ar HaKavanot), that the Ari prayed for a long time at his home with a quorum of ten without a Torah scroll — and one must therefore say he relied on the other congregations that were bringing out a Torah scroll, since what is done in them benefits his congregation too, as everything is joined together. In the same way, the Ben Ish Chai says that one who prays with the congregation but prolongs his prayer and misses the [leader's] repetition — his prayer is nevertheless complete by virtue of the secret of the repetition, since it is joined with that congregation's prayer.
He further brings a dispute: some wrote (Rav Emet LeYa'akov) that one who is God-fearing should say Vaya'avor and Nefilat Apayim privately on these days; the Ben Ish Chai had reservations about this, and agreed only with the suggestion to have it in mind through thought. And Rabbi Eliyahu Mani, may his Rock preserve him, wrote to him that an ancient custom in Beit El was to have all the intentions in mind, in the heart, between the repetition and the Kaddish.
takeaways: On days without confession/Nefilat Apayim, the [spiritual] unions occur by themselves through the holiness of the day; the custom of the pious is to have this in mind through thought alone.

A weekday when these were omitted due to a groom or circumcision is completed through the prayer of another congregation, since all prayers are joined and rise together (as with one who missed the repetition).
There is a dispute as to whether one should say 'Vaya'avor' and Nefilat Apayim privately; the main point is to have it in mind through thought, in the heart.

paragraphs: One must confess while standing, and likewise the additional supplications on Mondays and Thursdays — all while standing; and he should not lean upon anything that would cause him to fall if it were removed, unless he is elderly or ill, in which case he is permitted to lean on something. And if he sees the congregation confessing, even though he had already confessed, he should confess together with them. And it is written in Shalmei Tzibbur that people do not customarily act this way, and that they have grounds to rely on — see there. But it seems to me that, even though the custom has developed this way, it is proper that anyone who sees the congregation confessing should say 'We have sinned, we have committed iniquity, we have transgressed,' which is a general and brief confession. And one should not say the confession on Motza'ei Shabbat until after midnight. And the Chesed LaAlafim writes that perhaps the same applies to the conclusion of Rosh Chodesh, and the conclusion of Chanukah and Purim, and the like, since it is better to refrain from acting [when in doubt].

clarification.explanation: One must confess while standing, and likewise the additional supplications on Mondays and Thursdays — all while standing; and one should not lean on anything that would fall if removed, unless he is elderly or ill, in which case he is permitted to lean. And if he sees the congregation confessing — even though he has already confessed — he should confess together with them. And Shalmei Tzibbur writes that people do not customarily act this way and have grounds to rely upon; nevertheless, it seems to the Ben Ish Chai that it is proper that anyone who sees a congregation confessing should say at least 'We have sinned, we have committed iniquity, we have transgressed' — a general and brief confession. And one does not say the confession on Motza'ei Shabbat until after midnight; and the Chesed LaAlafim writes that perhaps the same applies to the conclusion of Rosh Chodesh, Chanukah, and Purim, and the like — since it is better to refrain [from an act in doubt].
takeaways: One confesses standing (and likewise the Monday/Thursday supplications), and does not lean unless elderly or ill.
One who sees a congregation confessing should join them, saying at least 'We have sinned, we have committed iniquity, we have transgressed.'
There is no confession on Motza'ei Shabbat until after midnight (and possibly the same at the conclusion of Rosh Chodesh/Chanukah/Purim).

paragraphs: It is forbidden to mention the Thirteen Attributes at night. Therefore, those who pray Minchah at the end of the day, near sunset — if by the time they reached the confession the time of the Maghrib call had already passed, which is exactly the end of the twelve [seasonal] hours — they should not say the Thirteen Attributes, but should say the confession alone.

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to mention the Thirteen Attributes at night. Therefore, those who pray the Minchah service at the end of the day, near sunset — if, by the time they reached the confession, the time of the 'Maghrib' [the Muslim call to the evening prayer, marking the end of the twelve seasonal daytime hours] had already passed — should not say the Thirteen Attributes, but only the confession alone.
takeaways: The Thirteen Attributes may not be said at night; one who prays Minchah too close to sundown, past the end of the day, says only the confession without the Thirteen Attributes.

paragraphs: An individual does not say the Thirteen Attributes, for they are a matter of sanctity that requires a quorum of ten. One who prays alone, when he comes to say the Thirteen Attributes after the confession, should say them with the cantillation notes, as one reading from the Torah — see the later authorities on this. I myself am accustomed, on Mondays and Thursdays when praying alone, to say the Thirteen Attributes after the confession with cantillation, but only up to 'as You made known to the humble one of old' and no further; and from 'and thus it is written in Your Torah,' etc., to the end of the Thirteen Attributes, I merely look at the siddur and have it in mind through thought alone — thus I have been accustomed for a number of years when praying alone on Mondays and Thursdays. However, afterward I saw in the handwritten book Keter Malkhut that it is written that an individual should not say the Thirteen Attributes in the language of the Torah at all, but is permitted to say them in the language of the [Aramaic] Targum, saying thus: 'And the Lord passed by before him and proclaimed: The Lord, the Lord, God, merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abundant in doing good and truth, keeping His goodness for a thousand generations, forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin, pardoning those who return to His Torah' — end of the Targum. And after this he should say the following petition: 'I beseech You, O Lord, the Living God, grant us abundantly a flow of light and blessing, grace, kindness, mercy, and strength; please, O Lord, the Redeeming God, crown us, gladden us' — end. And this petition's words are all constructed from the letters of the Thirteen Attributes, namely 'The Lord, the Lord, God, merciful and gracious,' etc. — end of the words of the aforementioned book Keter Malkhut. And I am accustomed to do so, following the thought-intention I have in mind for the Thirteen Attributes.

clarification.explanation: An individual is not permitted to say the Thirteen Attributes in the ordinary manner, because they are considered a 'matter of sanctity' requiring a quorum of ten. Therefore, one who prays alone, upon reaching the Thirteen Attributes after the confession, should say them with the Torah cantillation notes, as one reading from the Torah (this being a way to circumvent the problem of reciting them as an ordinary sacred matter). The Ben Ish Chai relates that he himself is accustomed, when praying alone on Mondays and Thursdays, to say only the beginning of 'Vaya'avor' with cantillation, up to 'as You made known to the humble one of old,' while from 'and thus it is written in Your Torah' to the end of the Thirteen Attributes he merely looks at the siddur and has it in mind through thought alone — so he was accustomed for many years. Later he found written in the manuscript book Keter Malkhut that an individual should not say the Thirteen Attributes in the language of the Torah at all, but is permitted to say them in Aramaic translation; and after the translation he should add a special petition whose every word is constructed from the letters of the Thirteen Attributes. The Ben Ish Chai notes that he is accustomed to do so, combined with the thought-intention he has in mind for the Thirteen Attributes.
takeaways: An individual does not say the Thirteen Attributes in the ordinary manner, since they are a matter of sanctity requiring a quorum; one may say them with Torah cantillation (as though reading from the Torah), or alternatively in Aramaic translation.

paragraphs: At the time one says 'Vaya'avor,' he should bow slightly, and stand upright at the [divine] Name, when he says 'The Lord, the Lord, God, merciful and gracious.' It is good to raise one's voice, on condition that people will not mock him for it — so writes the Chesed LaAlafim. And I asked our beloved friend, the Gaon and pious Rabbi Mahara Mani, may his Rock and Redeemer preserve him, to inform me of the custom of the congregation of the pious ones in Beit El, may it be built and established, in the holy city [Jerusalem], may it be built and established speedily in our days — and he wrote to me: 'The plain custom is to bow slightly at the words "and the Lord passed by before him," and at the word "and proclaimed" they raise their heads, and likewise at the words "The Lord, the Lord" they bow slightly' — see Shiyurei Berachah, section 138, and Shalmei Tzibbur, page 149, column 1. And according to the esoteric teaching, no reason for this is found explicitly; however, one who has learned the intentions (kavanot) precisely and wishes to find support for the custom can easily do so. And I received the tradition that at the words 'The Lord, the Lord' one should raise his feet [slightly, i.e., rise up on his toes], though I did not find this stated explicitly in the books of the halachic authorities; nevertheless I am accustomed to do so, for 'if it does not help, it will not harm' — end of his words, may his Rock preserve him.

clarification.explanation: At the time one says 'Vaya'avor' he should bow slightly, and stand upright at the [divine] Name — when he says 'The Lord, the Lord, God, merciful and gracious.' It is good to raise one's voice, provided that people will not mock him for it (Chesed LaAlafim). And the Ben Ish Chai asked Rabbi Eliyahu Mani, may his Rock preserve him, about the custom of the congregation of the pious in Beit El: the plain custom is to bow slightly at the words 'and the Lord passed by before him,' and at the word 'and proclaimed' to raise the head, and likewise to bow slightly at the words 'The Lord, The Lord.' And he wrote that according to the esoteric teaching no explicit reason is found for this, though one who has studied the intentions in detail can easily find support for it; and he added that he received the tradition to raise his feet at the words 'The Lord, The Lord,' though he did not find this stated explicitly in the works of the halachic authorities — and nevertheless he is accustomed to do so, since 'if it does not help, it will not harm.'
takeaways: At 'Vaya'avor' one bows slightly, and stands upright at the divine Name, 'The Lord, The Lord, God, merciful and gracious'; it is good to raise one's voice if this will not draw mockery.
The custom of Beit El: bowing at 'Vaya'avor... [the Lord] passed by,' and at 'The Lord, The Lord,' and raising the head at 'and proclaimed' (and some raise their feet at 'The Lord, The Lord').

paragraphs: One should be careful to give proper enunciation to the pause between the [first] 'the Lord' and the [second] 'the Lord,' for its secret is great, and one who does not properly enunciate it incurs a great punishment, as mentioned in the Chesed LaAlafim — see there, and see Sha'ar HaKavanot. See also the book Sefer HaLikkutim, printed in the holy city of Jerusalem, may it be built and established speedily in our days, in Parashat Ki Tisa, where the matter is elaborated at length, both this secret and the secret of the pause — see there.

clarification.explanation: One should be careful to give a slight pause between the first word 'the Lord' and the second word 'the Lord' in the verse 'The Lord, the Lord, God, merciful and gracious,' because there is a great secret in this, and one who does not make this distinction incurs a great punishment, as written in the Chesed LaAlafim and explained also in Sha'ar HaKavanot.
takeaways: One should give a slight pause between the two utterances of 'the Lord' in the verse of the Thirteen Attributes, on account of a great secret contained in that separation.

paragraphs: If the congregation is in distress over some kind of trouble, may it not come, then if a circumcision occurs on those days, it is good that the congregation say the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy with intention between the [act of] circumcision and the peri'ah — this is an especially efficacious matter, as mentioned in the Chesed LaAlafim.

clarification.explanation: If the congregation is in some kind of distress, may no trouble come, and on those days a circumcision takes place, it is good that the congregation say the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy with intention between the circumcision and the peri'ah — this is an especially efficacious matter, as written in the Chesed LaAlafim.
takeaways: In a time of communal distress, when there is a circumcision, it is recommended to say the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy with intention between the circumcision and the peri'ah — a special remedy for [invoking divine] mercy.

paragraphs: After the Thirteen Attributes, one says while standing, 'Merciful and gracious One, we have sinned before You; have mercy on us and save us,' and afterward, sitting, the psalm of David, 'To You, O Lord, I lift up my soul.' This psalm is called Nefilat Apayim (the falling upon the face), for it was originally instituted to be said while one bows his face upon his left arm; and one must be careful not to place his face literally within his left hand, for there is danger in this, Heaven forbid, but rather he should place his face upon his left arm, and cover his face with his tallit. One must be careful about Nefilat Apayim both in Shacharit and in Minchah. And it is written in the book of Kavanot [Sha'ar HaKavanot] that there are profound intentions in Nefilat Apayim — that one gives himself over to death, intending to bring down his soul to the place of death, which is the husks (kelipot), and to intend to extract from there the sparks that need rectification, and so forth. And one who merits to perform Nefilat Apayim properly, his reward is great, and his enemies fall before him. But due to our many sins, none among us knows how to do this matter, and we do not have the strength for it. Now, here in our city, Baghdad, may it be guarded and protected, it is not customary to place one's face upon one's arm at all — whether great man or small, whether scholar or simple person — and no one has in mind to give himself over for the sanctification of the Name, nor any other intention; rather, they simply say this psalm in a whisper. And what makes them so fearful and afraid about this is that they are concerned about the words of the holy Zohar, which said (Bemidbar, 102): 'Woe to him who says "To You, O Lord, I lift up my soul" and not all his words [correspond to his heart], but rather with a distant heart and without will' — and on this account a person must attach his soul and its wills to his Master, and not come before Him with mere words as they happen to come, as it is written (Psalms 101:7), 'He who speaks lies shall not stand before My eyes' — see there. Nevertheless, even according to the custom of our city, a person must be careful to say this psalm calmly, and in his heart understand what he brings forth with his lips. And I wrote to our beloved friend, the Gaon and pious Rabbi Mahara Mani, may his Rock preserve him, to inform me of the custom of the congregation of the pious in Beit El, may it be built and established, in Jerusalem, may it be rebuilt speedily, as to whether they place their faces upon their arms — and he wrote to me that they do not place their faces upon their arms, and do not change anything from the rest of the prayer service. Some give the reason that the intentions of Nefilat Apayim are lengthy and cannot be recalled by heart, and one would be forced to look into the siddur in one's hand [instead of covering the face]; and some say that the very tilting of the head upon the arm indicates the descent of the soul to the place of judgment, in order to bring the soul down into the depths of the husks to extract [the sparks]; and since we are fearful of bringing the soul down to the place of the husk, why then should we tilt to the side to indicate this matter of descent? — end of his words, may his Rock preserve him. And certainly it is good that every person refrain from placing his face upon his arm, and make no change whatsoever.

clarification.explanation: After the Thirteen Attributes one says while standing, 'Merciful and gracious One, we have sinned before You; have mercy on us and save us,' and afterward, sitting, the psalm 'To You, O Lord, I lift up my soul.' This psalm is called Nefilat Apayim, because it was originally instituted to be said while tilting the face upon the left arm — but one must be careful not to place the face literally inside the left hand (which involves danger), but rather upon the arm. One should cover the face with the tallit, and observe this both in Shacharit and Minchah. Sha'ar HaKavanot explains that Nefilat Apayim contains a profound intention of self-sacrifice — bringing the soul down to the place of the husks and extracting sparks of holiness from there — and one who merits doing this properly has a great reward, with his enemies falling before him. But because of our many sins we do not know how to do this, so in Baghdad — young and old, scholar and simple person alike — no one places his face on his arm at all, nor has any intention of self-sacrifice; rather, they only say the psalm in a whisper, out of fear stemming from the words of the holy Zohar, which warned that saying 'To You, O Lord, I lift up my soul' without true intention ('with a distant heart and without will') may be considered as 'speaking lies.' Nevertheless, one must be careful to say the psalm calmly and understand in the heart what is uttered by the lips. Also in Beit El, Jerusalem, they do not place the face on the arm, for the reason that the intentions are too lengthy to remember by heart, and also because if one is afraid to intentionally bring the soul down to the place of the husks, there is no point in tilting the head to symbolize that very descent. Therefore it is fitting that every person refrain from placing the face upon the arm and make no change in the text.
takeaways: In practice: one must not place the face literally inside the hand (danger), but at most upon the arm — and in Baghdad and Jerusalem the custom today is not to do so at all, but rather to say the psalm quietly while sitting.

The profound intentions of Nefilat Apayim (self-sacrifice, descending to extract sparks) are reserved for one who knows how to properly intend them; one who does not know should say the psalm calmly and with understanding.

paragraphs: Some are accustomed not to perform Nefilat Apayim except in a place that has an [Torah] Ark and a Torah scroll, or in the main sanctuary of the synagogue — but this is not correct; rather, according to the esoteric teaching, one should perform Nefilat Apayim in any place, even when praying alone. One should not perform Nefilat Apayim at night, and wherever there is doubt — such as during twilight (bein hashmashot) — one should not perform Nefilat Apayim, since it is better to refrain [from an act in doubt]. And after the psalm 'To You, O Lord, I lift up my soul,' one says 'Avinu Malkeinu' (Our Father, Our King) and so forth, which is an awesome prayer and supplication.

clarification.explanation: Some are accustomed not to perform Nefilat Apayim except in a place that has a Holy Ark and a Torah scroll, or in the main sanctuary — but this is an error. According to the esoteric teaching, one should perform Nefilat Apayim in any place, even when praying alone. One should not perform Nefilat Apayim at night, and likewise in any case of doubt (such as twilight), one should not perform it, on the principle that it is better to refrain. After the psalm 'To You, O Lord, I lift up my soul,' one says 'Avinu Malkeinu,' and so forth — an awesome prayer and supplication.
takeaways: Nefilat Apayim may be performed anywhere, even alone, and not only in a place with a Holy Ark; but it should not be performed at night or at a time of doubt.

paragraphs: When one says 'Ashrei' and 'Tehillah LeDavid,' he should have great intention in this psalm, especially in the verse 'You open Your hand.' And regarding what our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 4b) — that one who says 'Tehillah LeDavid' three times each day is assured that he is a son of the World to Come — this means: if he said it with proper intention of the heart, then it protects him to be a son of the World to Come. And when he says 'And a redeemer shall come to Zion, and to those in Jacob who turn from transgression,' he should have in mind that the initial letters of 'Go'el' and 'uleshavei fesha'' [redeemer, and those who turn from transgression] spell 'Guf' [body], and the initial letters of 'BeYa'akov Ne'um Hashem' and 'Va'ani' spell 'Banav' [His children/sons] — and one should intend by this that his 'children,' who descended to the external [husks] through the sin of wasted seed, will now, through his repentance, return to the 'treasury of souls' called by the name 'body,' and the redeemer will come — as mentioned in the words of our teacher, the Ari, of blessed memory.

clarification.explanation: When saying 'Ashrei' and 'Tehillah LeDavid' one should have great intention, especially in the verse 'You open Your hand.' What our Sages said — that one who says 'Tehillah LeDavid' three times a day is assured to be a son of the World to Come — means specifically when it is said with true intention of the heart; then it protects him to be a son of the World to Come. When saying 'U'va LeTziyon go'el ulshavei fesha beYa'akov' [And a redeemer shall come to Zion, to those in Jacob who turn from transgression], one should intend that the initial letters of 'go'el ulshavei fesha' spell 'guf' (body), and the initial letters of 'beYa'akov ne'um Hashem' [and 'va'ani' - and I] spell 'banav' (his children) — and intend that a person's 'children,' who descended to the husks ('external ones') through the sin of wasted seed, now return, through his repentance, to the 'treasury of souls' called 'body,' and the redeemer will come.
takeaways: The assurance of being 'a son of the World to Come' for one who says 'Tehillah LeDavid' three times daily is conditional on true intention of the heart in saying it.
In 'U'va LeTziyon' one should intend, by the secret of the initial letters, that even lost sparks (from the sin of wasted seed) can return to rectification through repentance.

paragraphs: The sanctity [Kedushah] of 'U'va LeTziyon' is called 'Kedushah DeSidra,' because the later authorities arranged it in the pattern of the Kedushah of the Amidah, as mentioned in Shibbolei HaLeket, which is brought in Beit Yosef — that once the enemies of Israel decreed against Israel that they should not say Kedushah in the prayer service, and they would post ambushers and wait until the congregation finished the Amidah with its repetition and then leave. Therefore they instituted saying an order of Kedushah here [at U'va LeTziyon]. And after the decree against the Kedushah of the Amidah and the Kedushah of Yotzer was annulled, they nevertheless instituted this Kedushah in the holy tongue and in Aramaic translation, corresponding to the two [previously threatened] Kedushot — and therefore it is called 'Kedushah DeSidra,' since it was arranged corresponding to the two Kedushot mentioned. And even though the decree was later annulled, they did not subsequently annul this Kedushah, because in truth there is a reason for it according to the esoteric teaching. And the reason the Men of the Great Assembly did not institute it originally is that the proper and rectified time for this institution had not yet arrived; and when the proper time arrived, the Holy One, blessed be He, brought about the aforementioned circumstance on account of which this Kedushah was instituted here — and therefore it was not annulled afterward even though the circumstance [that caused it] was annulled, because our Sages of blessed memory saw with their holy spirit that in truth it was fitting for there to be a Kedushah here, according to the esoteric teaching. There is another reason why it is called 'Kedushah DeSidra' — because it is a new institution that was not instituted by the Men of the Great Assembly together with the Kedushah of Yotzer and the Kedushah of the Amidah, but rather was instituted here because here is the secret of the descent of Malkhut [the Divine Kingship] into the World of Creation (Beri'ah), in the Sanctuary of the Holy of Holies — and therefore we now say 'Kadosh,' 'Baruch,' and 'Yimlokh le'olam va'ed,' in order to draw down the flow of holiness. 'DeSidra' means that it was instituted according to the order of the worlds, and we say it in the order corresponding to the worlds. And the custom is to say the Aramaic translation in a whisper, as is written in the Shulchan Aruch — and although our teacher Rabbi Chaim Vital, of blessed memory, wrote that our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, used to say it aloud, and I also heard that the custom of the pious ones in Beit El, may it be built and established, is not to be exacting about this, sometimes saying it in a whisper and sometimes aloud — here in Baghdad the custom is to be exacting about this, saying it specifically in a whisper, for 'if it does not help, it will not harm.'

clarification.explanation: The Kedushah of 'U'va LeTziyon' is called 'Kedushah DeSidra,' since the later authorities arranged it as a parallel to the Kedushah of the Amidah. The background: once the enemies of Israel decreed that Kedushah must not be said in prayer, and they would lie in ambush, waiting for the congregation to finish the repetition (including the Kedushah), and then leave. Therefore an additional order of Kedushah was instituted here — after the decree against the Kedushah of the Amidah and of Yotzer had been rescinded — to be said both in the holy tongue and in Aramaic translation, corresponding to the two Kedushot that had been forbidden and later restored. That is why it is called 'Kedushah DeSidra' — arranged corresponding to two Kedushot. Although the decree was later annulled, this Kedushah was not subsequently annulled, since it has a deep reason according to the esoteric teaching; and the reason the Men of the Great Assembly did not institute it from the start is that the proper time for this institution had not yet arrived, and when the time came, the Holy One, blessed be He, brought about the aforementioned episode of the decree so that this Kedushah would be instituted here — and therefore it was not later annulled even though the original cause was annulled, because our Sages saw with their holy spirit that it is truly fitting for there to be a Kedushah here, according to the esoteric teaching. Another reason for its name: it is a new institution that was not instituted together with the Kedushah of Yotzer and of the Amidah by the Men of the Great Assembly, but instituted here because this place expresses, in secret, the descent of Malkhut into the World of Creation, in the Sanctuary of the Holy of Holies — therefore here we say 'Kadosh,' 'Baruch,' and 'Yimlokh le'olam va'ed,' in order to draw down the flow of holiness, and it is called 'DeSidra' also because it was instituted according to the order of the worlds. It is customary to say the Aramaic translation in this Kedushah in a whisper, as fixed in the Shulchan Aruch, although there is testimony that the Ari said it aloud, and the pious of Beit El are not exacting about this; in Baghdad the custom is to be exacting and say the translation specifically in a whisper.
takeaways: The Kedushah of 'U'va LeTziyon' ('Kedushah DeSidra') was instituted as a substitute during the period when the Kedushah of prayer was forbidden, but it remained even after the ban was lifted, for a deep esoteric reason.
It is customary to say the Aramaic translation in this Kedushah in a whisper (the Baghdad custom), although there is testimony of other customs.

paragraphs: Before the psalms of the day, one says 'Today is the first day of the week' (Hayom yom echad beShabbat) if it is Sunday, and likewise, on the same principle, on Monday one says 'Today is the second day of the week,' and so too for Tuesday and the remaining days; only on Friday does one add the letter heh and say 'Today is the sixth day' with an extra heh; and on Sunday one is precise to say 'the first day of the holy Shabbat.' And one should intend, by this counting each day, to fulfill the commandment 'Remember the Sabbath day' (Exodus 20:8) — for our Sages, of blessed memory, said in the Sifrei (there) that it is a positive commandment from the Torah to count the days of the week by saying 'first day toward Shabbat, second day toward Shabbat,' etc., and so wrote the Ramban, of blessed memory — and the matter is to indicate that the weekdays are dependent upon and bound to the Shabbat, from which their illumination is drawn, as our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, wrote in Sha'ar HaKavanot. And on days when the confession is not said, the plain custom is not to say the psalm 'Ya'ankha' [May He answer you] nor the psalm 'Tefillah LeDavid' [A prayer of David] — and this is also the custom among the congregation of the pious ones in the holy city of Jerusalem, may it be rebuilt speedily; and we do not know a reason for [omitting] the psalm 'Tefillah LeDavid,' and it is said that this is a received tradition from the early authorities. And know that here, in our city Baghdad, may it be guarded and protected, the custom from ancient times was that on every public fast day when one recites the psalm belonging to it, and likewise on Motza'ei Yom Kippur and on Chanukah and Purim, which have their own associated psalms — they would not say 'Beit Ya'akov' or the psalm designated for the day of the week, but only the psalm belonging to that occasion alone. But, praise be to God, may He be blessed, I instituted the custom in all the synagogues of our city to say 'Beit Ya'akov' and the psalm belonging to that day of the week, and afterward say the psalm belonging to that occasion. And I also instituted that on that day, before the psalm of the day of the week, they should say 'Hayom yom...' — the song that the Levites used to say — just as is said on other days, whether on public fast days or on Motza'ei Yom Kippur; only on Chanukah did I institute that they should not say the song the Levites used to say on the platform, but should say only 'Today is such-and-such day, toward the holy Shabbat,' and say the weekly psalm followed by the Chanukah psalm, for I heard that this is the custom in the holy city [Jerusalem], may it be rebuilt speedily. And regarding Rosh Chodesh, I did not preach explicitly in public that they should also say 'Beit Ya'akov' and the weekly psalm — I only tell individuals who ask me that they should say 'Beit Ya'akov' and the weekly psalm before Musaf, and also say 'Today is such-and-such day, toward the holy Shabbat,' and after Musaf say 'Barchi Nafshi' as per the ancient custom; and some synagogues have had their cantors learn to do this publicly there. And the reason I did not preach about Rosh Chodesh in public and did not establish it as a fixed rule in all the synagogues, I have a reason for this. Therefore, any community elsewhere that follows a custom like the ancient custom that was here in our city — not to say 'Beit Ya'akov' and the weekly psalm on the aforementioned days — must change their custom and say 'Beit Ya'akov' and the weekly psalm, followed by the psalm belonging to the occasion of that day; and whoever does not do so causes a great deficiency in the institution that our Sages of blessed memory instituted in the prayer service.

clarification.explanation: Before the psalms of the day, one says 'Today is the first day toward Shabbat' if it is Sunday, and correspondingly for the rest of the days of the week; only on Friday does one add the letter heh and say 'Today is the sixth day' with an extra heh; and on Sunday one is precise to say 'the first day toward the holy Shabbat.' One should intend, in this daily count, to fulfill the positive Torah commandment of 'Remember the Sabbath day,' since our Sages said this is a positive commandment from the Torah — to count the days of the week and say 'first day toward Shabbat, second day toward Shabbat,' etc. — and so wrote the Ramban, in order to indicate that the weekdays are dependent upon and bound to Shabbat, from which their illumination is drawn. On days when confession is not said, the plain custom is also not to say the psalm 'Ya'ankha' or the psalm 'Tefillah LeDavid,' and so is the custom also among the pious of Jerusalem, though no clear reason is known for the omission of 'Tefillah LeDavid' — it is a received tradition from the early authorities. The Ben Ish Chai relates a further custom he instituted in Baghdad: previously, on public fast days, at the conclusion of Yom Kippur, on Chanukah, and on Purim, they would not say 'Beit Ya'akov' and the ordinary weekly psalm, but only the psalm specific to that day. He instituted in all the synagogues of his city that they should first say 'Beit Ya'akov' and the weekly psalm as usual, and afterward the psalm specific to that occasion — and also say the ordinary 'Today is...' before the weekly psalm. The exception is Chanukah, for which he instituted that they should not say the song the Levites used to say on the platform, but only 'Today is such-and-such day' and the weekly psalm, followed by the Chanukah psalm — as is customary in Jerusalem. Regarding Rosh Chodesh, he did not preach this publicly, but advised individuals who asked him to say 'Beit Ya'akov' and the weekly psalm before Musaf, and 'Today is...,' and after Musaf to say 'Barchi Nafshi' as per the ancient custom. In practice, the Ben Ish Chai ruled that any community elsewhere that follows the old custom [of omitting the weekly psalm] must change its custom and say 'Beit Ya'akov' and the weekly psalm followed by the occasion's psalm; and one who does not do so causes a great deficiency in the institution that our Sages established in the prayer service.
takeaways: Saying 'Today is [day]...' before the daily psalms fulfills the Torah's positive commandment of 'Remember the Sabbath day,' according to our Sages and the Ramban.

Everywhere one must say 'Beit Ya'akov' and the ordinary weekly psalm, followed by the special occasion's psalm (fast day, conclusion of Yom Kippur, Purim); a community that was accustomed to skip the weekly psalm must change its custom, and one who does not do so causes a great deficiency in the Sages' institution.

paragraphs: 'Ein KeElokeinu' (There is none like our God) is an awesome praise containing great intention according to the esoteric teaching, and one should say it calmly; and after it, the recitation of 'Pittum HaKetoret' (the compounding of the incense) with great intention — let him study it and praise it himself. Afterward one says the Kaddish for Israel, called 'Kaddish Yatoma' (the Orphan's Kaddish), which was instituted to be said by orphans for the repose of the soul of their father or mother; its benefit to the soul of the deceased is not merely to save it from judgment and punishment, but to elevate it from level to level — therefore it is said every day of the Yahrzeit even after many years have passed since the passing, and so was our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, accustomed to say it every year on the Yahrzeit of his father (since his mother was still alive). And here in our city, Baghdad, the custom is to say after this Kaddish, 'Rabbanan, Barchu et Hashem hamevorach' [Our Rabbis, bless the Lord who is blessed], but in the holy cities and other places they are not accustomed to say the word 'Rabbanan.' We are also accustomed here in our city, may it be guarded and protected, to say 'Rabbanan' also in the Kaddish that precedes 'Aleinu LeShabe'ach' in the evening service, and likewise we are accustomed to say 'Rabbanan' when called up to the Torah — and we have not changed this custom, even though most communities, especially in the lands of the West, are not accustomed to say 'Rabbanan,' since I have not seen that there is any harm or objection in this matter that would warrant changing the custom; therefore, every place that has been accustomed to do so should remain with its custom. And in my holy book Rav Pe'alim I wrote, with God's help, in a responsum, a reason for saying 'Rabbanan' in the Barchu that follows the Orphan's Kaddish: the Barchu that precedes Yotzer is from the institutions of the Men of the Great Assembly, who instituted it in the manner that it is said in Heaven, as brought in the Midrash; but here, the Men of the Great Assembly did not institute the saying of Barchu — rather, the later Sages instituted it. Therefore, one who says Barchu here says 'Rabbanan, Barchu' etc., meaning: 'with the permission of our Rabbis, I say Barchu et Hashem hamevorach' — and the same applies to the Barchu at the calling up to the Torah, which likewise was not instituted by the Men of the Great Assembly. See HaShomer Emet, section 10, letter alef — see there. And after answering Barchu, the congregation shall stand and say, with great intention, 'Aleinu LeShabe'ach,' which is a most exalted and awesome praise, and there is great need for it after the prayer that we have prayed, in order to nullify the grip of the external [powers/husks]; and by the bowing that we perform, bending the head and part of the body, we draw down the encompassing light in descent through all the worlds down to the entirety of the World of Action ('Asiyah'). One must say this entire praise while standing, and our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, warned that one should not remove his tzitzit and tefillin until the completion of 'the Lord is One and His Name is One' — and one should intend that this verse begins with the letter vav and ends with the letter dalet, which together are numerically ten, alluding to the ten manifestations of the Tetragrammaton in the spelling-out of the letter heh, called 'Ben' (which are called the 'ten sons' that will illuminate 'Leah' — alluded to in the initial letters of 'VeHayah Hashem LeMelekh' [And the Lord shall become King], which equals thirty-six, the numerical value of 'Leah,' with the Name Havayah in the middle alluding to the aforementioned manifestations). And if one is not praying with the congregation but hears the congregation saying 'Va'anachnu mishtachavim' [But we bow down], he too should bow down with them, even though there is no strict obligation in this as there is in the law of 'Modim.' And the Chesed LaAlafim writes that when one says 'to a god that cannot save,' he should pause briefly, and afterward say 'Va'anachnu mishtachavim.' And if it happened that one needs to answer Amen when the leader says 'who bow down to vanity and emptiness,' or likewise when he says 'and pray to a god that cannot save,' he should not answer Amen there. And the custom is to say, after the verse 'VeHayah Hashem LeMelekh...,' the verse 'VeHayah im shamo'a tishma leKol Hashem Elokecha' etc., until 'for I am the Lord your Healer.'

clarification.explanation: 'Ein KeElokeinu' is an awesome praise with great intention according to the esoteric teaching, and it should be said calmly; afterward, one says 'Pittum HaKetoret' with great intention. Then one says the Kaddish for Israel, called 'Kaddish Yatoma' (the Orphan's Kaddish), which was instituted for orphans to recite for the repose of their father's or mother's soul; its benefit is not only to save from judgment and punishment, but to elevate the soul from level to level — therefore it is said on every Yahrzeit even many years after the passing, and the Ari was accustomed to say it every year on his father's Yahrzeit. In Baghdad the custom is to say after this Kaddish, 'Rabbanan, Barchu et Hashem hamevorach' (with the word 'Rabbanan'), which is not the custom in Jerusalem and elsewhere; likewise in Baghdad they say 'Rabbanan' in the Kaddish before 'Aleinu LeShabe'ach' at the evening service, and when called up to the Torah — because in this Barchu (unlike the ordinary Barchu before Yotzer, instituted by the Men of the Great Assembly), the institution is from later Sages, so one says 'with the permission of our Rabbis, I say Barchu.' After answering Barchu, the congregation rises and says, with great intention, 'Aleinu LeShabe'ach,' which nullifies the grip of the external [powers]; and by the bowing (bending the head and part of the body) one draws down the 'encompassing' light through all the worlds down to the World of Action. One must say this entire praise standing, and should not remove tzitzit or tefillin until completing 'the Lord is One and His Name is One' — this verse begins with vav and ends with dalet, whose sum is ten, alluding to the ten manifestations of the Tetragrammaton in the spelled-out form of the letter heh (called 'Ben'), which illuminate 'Leah' (alluded to in the initial letters of 'VeHayah Hashem LeMelekh,' which also equals thirty-six, the numerical value of 'Leah,' with the Name Havayah in the middle alluding to those manifestations). One who is not praying with the congregation but hears them saying 'Va'anachnu mishtachavim' should also bow with them, though this is not a strict obligation as with 'Modim.' One should pause briefly before 'Va'anachnu mishtachavim' (after 'a god that cannot save'), and should not answer Amen on 'who bow down to vanity and emptiness' or on 'and pray to a god that cannot save.' It is customary to say, after 'VeHayah Hashem LeMelekh,' also the verse 'VeHayah im shamo'a tishma... until 'for I am the Lord your Healer.'
takeaways: In Baghdad they say 'Rabbanan' before the Barchu following the Orphan's Kaddish, before Aleinu LeShabe'ach, and when called to the Torah — since this Barchu was instituted by later Sages, not the Men of the Great Assembly.

'The Lord is One and His Name is One' (beginning with vav, ending with dalet = 10) alludes to the ten manifestations of the Tetragrammaton in the spelling of the letter heh, which illuminate 'Leah'; one should not remove tzitzit and tefillin before completing it.
Precision regarding Amen: one does not answer on 'who bow down to vanity and emptiness' or 'and pray to a god that cannot save.'
